exemplar.title: What strong work looks like
exemplar.intro: A strong pricing memo turns expressions into decisions — here is how one student priced a T-shirt printing business.

traits.trait: Writes profit as an expression first
traits.sample: My profit is 12n − (4n + 50): $12 per shirt sold minus $4 supplies per shirt and the $50 press rental.
traits.why: Each term is tied to a real cost, so the expression tells the story.

traits.sample: In month 3 I sold 40 shirts, so 12(40) − (4(40) + 50) = 480 − 210 = $270 profit.
traits.why: The substitution is shown line by line, making the answer checkable.

traits.sample: Orders doubled monthly from 5: 5 × 2⁴ = 80 shirts by month 5 — the exponent counts the doublings.
traits.why: Exponential growth is explained by what the exponent counts.

traits.sample: The bulk tier earns less per shirt but my table shows it wins after 60 shirts, so I recommended it for big orders.
traits.why: The recommendation comes from computed comparisons, not a hunch.
